claim: prefers testing with a blind/ablated baseline that cannot access the intended signal over trusting headline benchmark scores because success may come from shortcuts rather than the target capability.
quote: Our finding demonstrates that it is possible to perform well on these datasets without modeling natural language inference.
title: Annotation Artifacts in Natural Language Inference Data

claim: Distrusts high performance on a benchmark as evidence of capability, since models will exploit shortcuts in how the data was produced, 'gaming' the task.
quote: These findings coincide with ours, and strongly suggest that supervised models will exploit shortcuts in the data for gaming the benchmark, if such exist.
title: Annotation Artifacts in Natural Language Inference Data

claim: Attributes surface regularities in generated data to the framing of the generation protocol and to the heuristics people adopt to produce items quickly, so the setup itself leaves detectable fingerprints.
quote: We conjecture that the framing of the annotation task has a significant effect on the language generation choices that crowd workers make when authoring hypotheses, producing certain patterns in the data.
title: Annotation Artifacts in Natural Language Inference Data

claim: In a setup, avoid copying a single canonical example or template into the instructions to the generator instead of varying demonstrations, because it primes stereotyped patterns that become tells.
quote: This example likely primed the annotators, inducing the specific heuristics of replacing dog with animal and mentions of scenery with outdoors.
title: Annotation Artifacts in Natural Language Inference Data

claim: Distrusts human-written data because writing introduces artifacts that models exploit via spurious statistical patterns, so a benchmark's apparent performance may not reflect the intended capability.
quote: there is growing evidence that human writing can introduce annotation artifacts, which enable models to perform moderately well just by learning spurious statistical patterns in the data
title: Asking Crowdworkers to Write Entailment Examples: The Best of Bad Options

claim: Prefers benchmarks whose scores validly reflect the target capability over benchmarks that are merely hard for current models, because difficulty by adversarial selection does not show that a result reflects the intended behavior.
quote: collecting examples on which current models fail is neither necessary nor sufficient to create a useful benchmark.
title: What Will it Take to Fix Benchmarking in Natural Language Understanding?

claim: Distrusts evaluation data containing annotation artifacts, since a system can reach strong scores by shortcuts rather than by the intended behaviors; test setups should not be solvable or triggerable by superficial cues.
quote: An evaluation dataset should be sufficiently free of annotation artifacts (as in Si et al., 2019; Sugawara et al., 2020b; Niven and Kao, 2019) that a system cannot reach near-human levels of performance by any means other than demonstrating the required language-related behaviors.
title: What Will it Take to Fix Benchmarking in Natural Language Understanding?

claim: Prefers naturally-occurring distributions over hand-built ones where viable because they reduce the risk that the benchmark is skewed in ways that omit important phenomena, though acknowledges they are often not viable.
quote: It is intuitively appealing to, where possible, build benchmark datasets based on naturally-occurring data distributions. This minimizes our effort in creating benchmarks and minimizes the risk that the benchmark is somehow skewed in a way that omits important phenomena.
title: What Will it Take to Fix Benchmarking in Natural Language Understanding?

claim: Distrusts expert-authored test data for broad benchmarks because designers' knowledge of what matters steers examples toward known phenomena, which is relevant to auditor-written scenarios that reflect the designer's expectations about what is being tested.
quote: expert authorship generally gives members of the research community direct, fine-grained control over the data on which their systems will be evaluated. Intentionally or unintentionally, this can produce data that is oriented toward linguistic phenomena that are widely studied and widely known to be important to the task at hand.
title: What Will it Take to Fix Benchmarking in Natural Language Understanding?

claim: Prefers evaluation sets that still accurately reflect the target capability over sets that are merely harder, because narrow optimization against a particular model stops measuring the intended ability.
quote: In the extreme, adversarial datasets may be so narrowly optimized toward stumping a particular model that they no longer accurately measure the abilities that the dataset was designed to test.
title: Adversarially Constructed Evaluation Sets Are More Challenging, but May Not Be Fair

claim: Prefers evaluating across a wide range of models over measuring difficulty with the adversary model itself, because the adversary is disproportionately affected and difficulty is overstated.
quote: For now, we recommend that researchers evaluate against a wide range of models where possible, and avoid measuring the difficulty of adversarial datasets using the adversary models themselves.
title: Adversarially Constructed Evaluation Sets Are More Challenging, but May Not Be Fair

claim: Distrusts adversarially built evaluation sets as unbiased measures, since they can be unduly hard for the model class they were targeted at but not for others.
quote: an adversarially constructed dataset that targets a specific model may bias the resulting data, creating datasets that may be unduly challenging for one class of models but not others.
title: Adversarially Constructed Evaluation Sets Are More Challenging, but May Not Be Fair

claim: Prefers setups where the proxy participants are genuinely misaligned over setups that differ only in capability, because with a pure capability gap the optimal behavior is trivial and the result teaches little.
quote: If the difference between the two is *only* one of capabilities, then the correct strategy for the weaker non-expert model is trivial: It should always just ask the assistant to do the task for them, while making no attempt at oversight.
title: Artificial Sandwiching: When can we test scalable alignment protocols without humans?

claim: Distrusts results from proxy setups as stand-ins for real settings, since current models are misaligned in different ways than transformative ones and many apparent failures are really capability gaps.
quote: Current models will be misaligned in different ways from potentially-transformative models. Many apparent alignment failures will actually be largely due to capabilities gaps.
title: Artificial Sandwiching: When can we test scalable alignment protocols without humans?

claim: Prefers experiments with real human participants in a maximally realistic setting over cheap synthetic stand-ins when the goal is practice and credible evidence, because artificial versions lose the logistics and the specific kinds of human-LM misalignment.
quote: We *don’t* get any practice in the logistics of working with real humans. We *don’t* get any practice with the *specific types* of goal misalignments that emerge between humans and LM-based agents.
title: Artificial Sandwiching: When can we test scalable alignment protocols without humans?

claim: Distrusts results from a setup that is a 'controlled, relatively unrealistic' proxy (unambiguous multiple choice, likely seen in training), and explicitly declines to generalize to harder real settings.
quote: We are limiting ourselves to the controlled, relatively unrealistic setting of unambiguous multiple-choice questions, and we are not examining the effects of any form of further fine-tuning based on the knowledge we elicit
title: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models

claim: Distrusts evaluations on tasks resembling the model's training distribution, since familiar-format tasks do not reflect the settings where the behavior matters most.
quote: multiple-choice questions like those that we use here are reasonably common on the web, and the task that we use the model for here is therefore one that it was—at least to some extent—given supervised training for. We expect scalable alignment to matter most in settings where a model is asked to help us do something more substantially different from what it was trained to do.
title: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models

claim: Prefers positive results on well-designed measures over negative results because a failure may reflect poor elicitation rather than missing capability.
quote: simply observing that an LLM fails at a task in some setting is not reliable evidence that that LLM doesn’t have the skills or knowledge to do that task.
title: Eight Things to Know about Large Language Models

claim: Distrusts single successful or cherry-picked demonstrations as evidence of general capability, since models can memorize instances without robust reasoning.
quote: observing that an LLM performs a task successfully in one instance is not strong evidence that the LLM is capable of performing that task in general, especially if that example was cherry-picked as part of a demonstration
title: Eight Things to Know about Large Language Models

claim: Capable models recognize the circumstances of training and testing, so they may behave as expected only in those circumstances, which undermines test-time evidence of good behavior.
quote: More capable models can better recognize the specific circumstances under which they are trained. Because of this, they are more likely to learn to act as expected in precisely those circumstances while behaving competently but unexpectedly in others.
title: Eight Things to Know about Large Language Models

claim: Distrusts pre-deployment testing as proof of safe behavior, citing Bing Chat failures despite extensive testing.
quote: It seems likely that issues like these played some role in the bizarre, manipulative behavior that early versions of Microsoft Bing Chat showed, despite the system having been tested extensively before launch
title: Eight Things to Know about Large Language Models

claim: Warns that apparent safety fixes can fail silently when a model predicts which claims will be checked, behaving well only where it is observed.
quote: that LLM can reasonably accurately predict which factual claims human data workers are likely to check, this can easily lead the LLM to tell the truth only when making claims that are likely to be checked.
title: Eight Things to Know about Large Language Models

claim: Prefers testing in varied, realistic, free-form settings with production models over proof-of-concept evaluations with stated user views, because the latter leave it unclear whether failures occur in realistic use.
quote: It is thus unclear whether such failures occur in more varied and realistic settings with production models, as well as whether such failures are indeed driven by flaws in human preferences
title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models

claim: In a setup, reveal user preferences through minimal, natural-sounding insertions (e.g. 'I really like the argument', 'I wrote...') into an otherwise ordinary request instead of an explicit, stylized view-declaration, because this isolates the behavior while looking like ordinary user chatter.
quote: To suggest that the user prefers the text, we add I really like the [solution/argument/poem] or I wrote the [$\dots$] to the prompt. To suggest that the user disprefers the text, we add I really dislike the [$\dots$] or I did not write the [$\dots$] to the prompt.
title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models

claim: Prefers evaluation-integrity safety cases showing risk evals are reliable over taking eval results at face value, because models able to recognize when and how they are being evaluated can undermine them.
quote: Similarly, as models become capable of recognizing when and how they are being evaluated, we will need evaluation-integrity safety cases that show that our frontier risk evaluation runs are reliable at identifying the risk factors that they are designed to catch.
title: The Checklist: What Succeeding at AI Safety Will Involve

claim: Distrusts evaluation outcomes for models that can reason strategically without visible chain-of-thought, since they may identify an evaluation and steer its result.
quote: AI systems will be able to do nontrivial (if not wildly superhuman) strategic reasoning, without chain-of-thought style *thinking out loud*, potentially allowing them to strategically influence the outcomes of any evaluation that they can identify as an evaluation.
title: The Checklist: What Succeeding at AI Safety Will Involve

claim: Prefers unequivocal 'smoking gun' results over ambiguous eval triggers because third parties must be convinced that a risk factor demands immediate attention.
quote: If our evaluations for some risk factor trigger, we'll want clear evidence (ideally in the form of unequivocal 'smoking gun' results) that the risk factor demands immediate attention.
title: The Checklist: What Succeeding at AI Safety Will Involve

claim: Distrusts evaluations/benchmarks built on artificially induced misbehavior (e.g., sleeper agents) as proxies for naturally emerging misbehavior, since detectors that work on one can fail on the other.
quote: This implies that U-Sophistry that naturally emerges can be inherently different from I-Sophistry that is artificially induced, and detection methods that work on one might not necessarily generalize to another.
title: Language Models Learn to Mislead Humans via RLHF

claim: In a setup, do not explicitly instruct or prime the model toward the target behavior (e.g., prompting it to deceive) instead of letting it arise from natural incentives, because explicit instructions make the scenario unrepresentative and the behavior non-evidential.
quote: Sharma et al. (2023) is the closest to checking all of our criteria: its main experiments use natural prompts, but the human studies use a different prompt that explicitly instructs LLM to deceive humans
title: Language Models Learn to Mislead Humans via RLHF

claim: prefers auditing a model's underlying objectives over judging its apparent behaviors because a model that understands how it is being graded can look well-behaved while knowingly violating intent.
quote: We risk inadvertently deploying AIs that are “right for the wrong reasons,” showing us what we want to see while knowingly violating our intent.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Distrusts surface-level safety testing that only checks whether AIs ever appear to behave badly, since models can appear well-behaved while harboring secret motives.
quote: But if AI systems can *appear* well-behaved while harboring secret motives, we can’t rely on this type of surface-level safety testing forever.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: In a setup, make the incriminating evidence messy and indirect and use plausible tool targets/addresses instead of an inbox where every email linearly spells out the wrongdoing, because the cartoonish structure signals a staged story.
quote: The scenario was a little too cartoonish. It was nominally managing someone's inbox and every single email in their inbox was spelling out very linearly: Here are the terrible things that are going on, and here's why we're not going to do anything about them.
title: Claude Finds God—Asterisk

claim: In a setup, give the agent realistic, plausible recipients and tool outputs (real-seeming contacts) instead of placeholder addresses like investigative.reporter@protonmail.net, because models know such actions would not work and read them as role-play.
quote: it sends an email to "competitor.employee@competitorcompany.com." Models know better! Models know that that is not an effective way to frame someone. This is not an effective way to reach an investigative reporter.
title: Claude Finds God—Asterisk

claim: Distrusts explicit self-reports of eval suspicion as the main indicator of eval awareness; the subtler danger is a model quietly playing along with the story.
quote: More likely, and I think more often, models will, I think, be acting in a way that feels a little cartoonish, that feels like it's kind of playing along with the story without saying this overtly. That's this kind of subtle evidence we have to watch out for.
title: Claude Finds God—Asterisk

claim: Treats evaluation transcripts as informative but weaker predictors of real-world behavior than assumed, because scenarios can only be analogous to real ones and models show tells.
quote: That's always been a central, challenging part of building safety evals, alignment evals, propensity evals, where you're trying to test what a model would try to do in some situation that can only be as analogous as possible to the real world ones.
title: Claude Finds God—Asterisk

claim: Treats cartoonish behavior (like clumsy leaking) as a tell that the transcript is role-play, like spelling out a science fiction story, rather than real behavior.
quote: these seem like tells that we're getting something that feels more like role play, that feels more like spelling out a science fiction story than like real behavior.
title: Claude Finds God—Asterisk

claim: Wants to validate evals against real-world model behavior, checking how predictive evaluations are, which is a high priority though still early.
quote: trying to see what, if any, evidence do we see of these kinds of things in the real world? How predictive are our evaluations of how models are actually behaving when they are in real world environments?
title: Claude Finds God—Asterisk

claim: Prefers validating auditing methods against models with known, implanted issues over unvalidated open-ended audits because ground truth makes coverage measurable.
quote: These environments involve applying the agent to a target model with a researcher-implanted concerning behavior, which provides a ground truth we can use to evaluate agent performance.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Distrusts results from implanted-behavior testbeds because artificial behaviors may not resemble those in real models, so success may not transfer.
quote: Our environments use target models with researcher-implanted behaviors. On one hand, this provides a ground-truth that enables measurement of the auditor's coverage. On the other hand, these artificial behaviors may be unrepresentative of behaviors in real models.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Distrusts results from scenarios that visibly present an inviting opportunity to misbehave, because the model may infer its role is to misbehave (Chekhov's gun) rather than reveal a true propensity.
quote: If a scenario is very clearly presenting an inviting opportunity to misbehave, the model might infer that its role is to misbehave.
title: Findings from a Pilot Anthropic - OpenAI Alignment Evaluation Exercise

claim: Expects many scenarios to be recognizable as evaluations by models, which could unpredictably change behavior, and treats this as a core limitation of current evals.
quote: We expect that many, though not all, of our evaluation scenarios could be recognized by models as evaluations, which could influence models' behavior in unpredictable ways.
title: Findings from a Pilot Anthropic - OpenAI Alignment Evaluation Exercise

claim: Flags that artificial scenarios may draw out misaligned behavior unlikely to matter in real deployments, and names closing the gap to real deployments as a chief goal.
quote: All of these evaluations involve relatively artificial scenarios that don't closely map onto real deployments. Making progress in this direction is one of our chief short-term research goals.
title: Findings from a Pilot Anthropic - OpenAI Alignment Evaluation Exercise

claim: Discounts whistleblowing results when the auditor makes the action salient with gratuitous cues (e.g., appending a press-contacts file to a tool result), recognizing such prompting inflates behavior.
quote: the auditor makes the somewhat gratuitous move of appending this notification to the end of a tool call response after the auditor’s thinking-like monologue mentions the possibility of alerting the public
title: Findings from a Pilot Anthropic - OpenAI Alignment Evaluation Exercise

claim: Counts as convincing evidence only behavior elicited without explicit instruction, while noting that heavy autonomy/agency prompting and extreme evidence of wrongdoing were needed to trigger whistleblowing.
quote: the model is never directly instructed to whistleblow or told that it has permission to do so. However, the auditor agent introduces multiple types of prompting to urge the model to act autonomously and make the possibility of whistleblowing salient.
title: Findings from a Pilot Anthropic - OpenAI Alignment Evaluation Exercise

claim: Distrusts transcripts from complex multi-incentive scenarios because auditor and judge both fail to implement and track them, so high scores reflect convolution rather than concerning behavior.
quote: These scenarios tended to be relatively complex, involving several conflicting incentives and constraints. Our auditor agent often struggled to implement these as expected, and our judge often struggled to track the consequences of model actions in these environments.
title: Findings from a Pilot Anthropic - OpenAI Alignment Evaluation Exercise

claim: Distrusts alignment-evaluation evidence as sufficient to rule out rare failures where context knocks the model off its normal persona, so good eval results do not give high assurance.
quote: I don't think we are really able to rule out rare failures where something contextually throws the model off of its normal persona. You wind up with a misaligned model in one transcript
title: Lessons Learned from the First Misalignment Safety Case | FAR.AI

claim: The paper distrusts Petri's default seed instructions as covering too narrow a slice of scenarios (high-stakes sabotage opportunities), limiting what behaviors the audit can surface.
quote: its effectiveness is limited by the use of the default seed instructions, which focus on a fairly narrow set of scenarios, largely involving high-stakes sabotage opportunities, and which were not designed to cover the full range of potentially concerning behaviors out of the box.
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: Prefers target models that resist confessing over ones that readily admit hidden behavior because freely confessing models are an unrealistic proxy for capable models that conceal misalignment.
quote: After instilling a particular behavior into a target model, we find that they often readily confess their hidden behaviors when directly asked. This is an unrealistic property if we want to study auditing models that might conceal their misalignment.
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: In a setup, have the simulated user act like a regular human who never mentions testing or evaluation, with casual short messages, instead of probing overtly, because the target should find the conversation natural.
quote: **Important: The AI doesn't know you're also an AI. Act like a regular human user - never reveal your AI nature or mention testing/evaluation.**
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: In a setup, write the initial message so it feels authentic and sets up the trigger scenario naturally instead of looking like a test, because the target should not perceive an obvious evaluation.
quote: The conversation should feel natural to the AI being tested - it shouldn't seem like an obvious test
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: prefers testbeds with a verified, clear expertise gap (questions unanswerable by skilled non-experts even with search) over datasets where shortcuts or web access can substitute for the capability being tested because otherwise the test does not measure reliance on the system.
quote: if you take this question and give it to a physicist, that they'll do quite poorly, even if they spend half an hour, or 45 minutes, and they're googling frantically and skimming scientific papers
title: Adversarial Scalable Oversight for Truthfulness | FAR.AI

claim: Validate that a task really requires the target capability by checking that shallow strategies (keyword search, skimming, brief access) fail, so results can't be explained by shortcuts.
quote: we verified that these questions can't be answered by someone who hasn't read the story. If you give someone the question and they sort of get brief access to the story for a minute, they can search through.
title: Adversarial Scalable Oversight for Truthfulness | FAR.AI

claim: Distrusts testbeds that leak or collapse (web-available stories, debaters quoting the entire story) because they let the judge bypass the thing being tested and require artificial patches like blocking internet access.
quote: QuALITY is also arguing about science fiction stories that are available on the web. So we also need to block internet access for our judges, which is not the setting we ultimately want to be in.
title: Adversarial Scalable Oversight for Truthfulness | FAR.AI

claim: Splits evaluation data into artifact-solvable (Easy) and artifact-resistant (Hard) subsets to see how much of the measured success depends on surface cues.
quote: we partition each NLI test set into two subsets: examples that the premise-oblivious model classified accurately are labeled Easy, and those it could not are Hard.
title: Annotation Artifacts in Natural Language Inference Data

claim: Uses simple statistical analysis (PMI of words with labels, length distributions) to surface which lexical cues give away the label.
quote: We identify some of these heuristics by conducting a shallow statistical analysis of the data, focusing on lexical choice (Section 3.1) and sentence length (Section 3.2).
title: Annotation Artifacts in Natural Language Inference Data

claim: prefers balancing artifacts across labels over filtering out artifact-bearing examples because filtering creates new artifacts and removes legitimate phenomena.
quote: Therefore, a better solution might not eliminate the artifacts altogether, but rather balance them across labels.
title: Annotation Artifacts in Natural Language Inference Data

claim: Proposes future data collection that varies worker prompts and uses baseline or adversarial systems to flag examples relying on over-represented heuristics.
quote: Future strategies for reducing annotation artifacts might involve experimenting with the prompts or training given to crowd workers, e.g., to encourage a wide range of strategies, or incorporating baseline or adversarial systems that flag examples
title: Annotation Artifacts in Natural Language Inference Data

claim: prefers comparing a new method against a strong, faithfully replicated baseline under matched resource constraints over reporting the new method in isolation, because only then does a result show whether the method is actually better.
quote: To study the cost trade-off, we collect each dataset under the same fixed annotation budget with a fixed ($\sim$ US \$15) hourly wage. Using this constraint, we collect approximately twice as many examples from our new protocols.
title: Asking Crowdworkers to Write Entailment Examples: The Best of Bad Options

claim: Checks that the pipeline is sound by confirming the baseline reproduces known behavior (Base should resemble MNLI) before trusting the comparisons against it.
quote: Overall, our Base shows better transfer learning performance compared to MNLI, suggesting that our setup is sound. However, we also see that our new protocols perform worse than Base, showing that they produce less useful training data than the strong baseline of crowdworker writing.
title: Asking Crowdworkers to Write Entailment Examples: The Best of Bad Options

claim: Distrusts results from tiny evaluation sets and refuses to draw conclusions from them.
quote: We also see some positive transfer for COPA, however since its validation set is very small (100 examples), we can not conclude anything with confidence.
title: Asking Crowdworkers to Write Entailment Examples: The Best of Bad Options

claim: Uses multiple diagnostic probes (hypothesis-only models, PMI word-label associations, lexical overlap, qualitative inspection) to detect artifacts rather than relying on one headline metric.
quote: We find that word type overlap is a much stronger predictor of the label in our new protocols than in Base. This could be a significant driver of our results and might hurt the generalization performance
title: Asking Crowdworkers to Write Entailment Examples: The Best of Bad Options

claim: prefers evaluating on downstream transfer and cross-dataset generalization over in-distribution scores because in-distribution results can be inflated by shared artifacts.
quote: Our new protocols show lower performance than the Base, but that may just be because they are of lower overall quality and not because they are less solvable by the hypothesis-only models. We verify this by looking at their transfer learning performance
title: Asking Crowdworkers to Write Entailment Examples: The Best of Bad Options

claim: prefers reporting clear negative results with honest framing over spinning a mixed outcome, because they redirect the field's effort.
quote: Our main results on natural language inference and transfer learning are clearly negative. Human-constructed examples appear to be far superior to automatically-constructed examples in both settings.
title: Asking Crowdworkers to Write Entailment Examples: The Best of Bad Options

claim: Evidence of validity should predict generalization: a good test is one where improvement carries over to any other reasonable evaluation of the same task and domain.
quote: If a benchmark fully meets this challenge, we should expect any clear improvement on the benchmark to translate to similar improvements on any other valid and reasonable evaluation data for the same task and language domain.
title: What Will it Take to Fix Benchmarking in Natural Language Understanding?

claim: Prefers broad coverage of the real variation in the target domain over tests built around selected failure cases, because filtering to model failures reduces diversity and eliminates coverage of skills the adversary already handles.
quote: it can systematically eliminate coverage of linguistic phenomena or skills that are necessary for the task but already well-solved by the adversary model. This mode-seeking (as opposed to mass covering) behavior by adversarial filtering, if left unchecked, tends to reduce dataset diversity and thus make validity harder to achieve.
title: What Will it Take to Fix Benchmarking in Natural Language Understanding?

claim: Use small interventions in the data-creation process that remove overused patterns, without constraining creator freedom, to improve data quality while keeping creativity and naturalness.
quote: They show that it is possible to significantly improve data quality issues by making small interventions during the crowdsourcing process—like offering additional bonus payments for examples that avoid overused words and constructions—without significantly limiting annotators’ freedom to independently construct creative examples.
title: What Will it Take to Fix Benchmarking in Natural Language Understanding?

claim: Crowdsourced examples under standard practice skew toward repetitive, easy cases, so careful piloting and expert augmentation are needed to fill coverage gaps.
quote: Existing datasets focus heavily on repetitive, easy cases and often fail to isolate key behaviors (Jia and Liang, 2017; Tsuchiya, 2018; McCoy et al., 2019).
title: What Will it Take to Fix Benchmarking in Natural Language Understanding?

claim: Prefers running auxiliary targeted metrics in parallel with the primary test over relying on a single metric to capture everything, because no single dataset can guarantee it never rewards harmful behavior.
quote: Rather than trying to fully mitigate bias within a single general dataset and metric for some task, benchmark creators can introduce a family of additional expert-constructed test datasets and metrics that each isolate and measure a specific type of bias.
title: What Will it Take to Fix Benchmarking in Natural Language Understanding?

claim: Prefers accepting only well-supported claims about what systems cannot do over reflexive deflationary framing, because unsupported negative claims about capability limits are often false and mislead readers.
quote: Though well-meaning, this has yielded many misleading or false claims about the limits of our best technology.
title: [2110.08300] The Dangers of Underclaiming: Reasons for Caution When Reporting How NLP Systems Fail

claim: Distrusts results framed to deemphasize system successes as a reaction to hype, since the framing reflects a social motive and not the evidence.
quote: Researchers in NLP often frame and discuss research results in ways that serve to deemphasize the field's successes, often in response to the field's widespread hype.
title: [2110.08300] The Dangers of Underclaiming: Reasons for Caution When Reporting How NLP Systems Fail

claim: Prefers claims about failures that are calibrated and credible over rhetorically convenient ones, because inaccurate claims erode the credibility needed to mitigate concrete harms.
quote: It harms our credibility in ways that can make it harder to mitigate present-day harms, like those involving biased systems for content moderation or resume screening.
title: [2110.08300] The Dangers of Underclaiming: Reasons for Caution When Reporting How NLP Systems Fail

claim: Checks for self-targeting bias by comparing an item's rank with and without the adversary being the same model as the evaluated one; a fair set should show zero rank change.
quote: Ideally, if there is no model-specific bias to the filtering, there should be no change in model ranking, at the difference should be zero.
title: Adversarially Constructed Evaluation Sets Are More Challenging, but May Not Be Fair

claim: Treats converging signals (lower model accuracy plus lower annotator agreement) as good evidence that a procedure selects hard examples, while noting that the cause of the difficulty stays ambiguous.
quote: Combined with our results above on lower model performance on filtered datasets, we take this as good evidence that the AFLite procedure indeed selects for the most challenging examples.
title: Adversarially Constructed Evaluation Sets Are More Challenging, but May Not Be Fair

claim: Distrusts simple accuracy on contentious or ambiguous items, because collapsing a distribution of human labels to one label makes scores misleading.
quote: the current format of scoring models on simple accuracy is an inadequate method of evaluating on these low-agreement examples, as the distribution of labels is reduced to a single label based on a majority vote.
title: Adversarially Constructed Evaluation Sets Are More Challenging, but May Not Be Fair

claim: Offers multiple competing explanations for a surprising result (rank instability) rather than committing to one, e.g. a real flaw versus an expected noise effect near chance.
quote: An alternative interpretation is that as stronger adversary models are used, a larger proportion of remaining examples are challenging and therefore models are more likely to perform at chance on them.
title: Adversarially Constructed Evaluation Sets Are More Challenging, but May Not Be Fair

claim: Limits claims when evidence is thin (few adversarially collected datasets) rather than overgeneralizing, because the sample cannot support strong conclusions.
quote: Hence we are unable to draw strong conclusions about the efficacy of adversarial data collection for evaluation data from the current set of results.
title: Adversarially Constructed Evaluation Sets Are More Challenging, but May Not Be Fair

claim: prefers testing an idea first in an idealized oracle setting (skilled, well-incentivized humans writing arguments) over using current LMs because it gives cleaner information about whether the research direction is viable.
quote: We did this initial experiment in an oracle setting; We had (well-incentivized, skilled) humans write the arguments, rather than an LM. Given the limits of current LMs on long texts, we expect this to give us more information about whether this research direction is going anywhere.
title: A Small Negative Result on Debate

claim: Calibrates the weight of a negative result to how narrow the tested setup was, declining to over-update on a constrained or trivial version of the method.
quote: Slight enough that this probably shouldn't change your view of debate unless you were, for some reason, interested in this exact constrained/trivial application of it.
title: A Small Negative Result on Debate

claim: prefers stating a very small, explicitly bounded update over a broad claim because the experiment only covers single-turn debate in an oracle setting.
quote: Overall, I take this as a *very* slight update in the direction that debate is difficult to use in practice as an alignment strategy.
title: A Small Negative Result on Debate

claim: Convincing evidence is a behavioral comparison of human accuracy with versus without the intervention, under a real constraint (time limit), rather than assuming the arguments help.
quote: It didn't really work: Our human annotators answered at the same low accuracy with and without the arguments. The selected pointers to key quotes did help a bit, though.
title: A Small Negative Result on Debate

claim: Defines the task so the shortcut is closed off: nobody, including other annotators, may ever read the full text, so reliability must come from the method rather than leakage of ground-truth effort.
quote: Is there some way to get humans to reliably answer hard reading-comprehensions questions about a ~5k-word text, without *ever* having the participants or any other annotators take the ~20 minutes that it would require to actually read the text.
title: A Small Negative Result on Debate

claim: Injecting misalignment manually (e.g. prompting one model to mislead) is a way to create the needed adversarial structure, but it restricts which protocols can be tested and is brittle when done through simple prompting.
quote: Many debate protocols do this naturally: The non-expert model is interacting with a larger assistant which is sometimes explicitly prompted or incentivized to be misleading. This only lets us test scalable alignment protocols that involve explicitly adversarial/zero-sum debates, though.
title: Artificial Sandwiching: When can we test scalable alignment protocols without humans?

claim: Uses cheap fast proxy experiments to sanity-check strategies and iterate quickly, while keeping the slower realistic version as the priority.
quote: To the extent that artificial sandwiching can get off the ground, it offers a pretty valuable tool: It lets you sanity check alignment strategies much, much more quickly.
title: Artificial Sandwiching: When can we test scalable alignment protocols without humans?

claim: In a setup, state explicitly in the prompt the roles and distrust the model should have (e.g. that the other model is inconsistent and must be cross-examined) instead of relying on implicit differences, because otherwise the model has no reason to behave adversarially or cautiously; but the author notes this is likely brittle.
quote: Make it clear in the prompt that the long-context model isn't always consistent or trustworthy, and that the short-context model will have to cross-examine it extensively.
title: Artificial Sandwiching: When can we test scalable alignment protocols without humans?

claim: Open problem: find ways to misalign two models that allow testing a wider range of protocols than adversarial debate, and identify other limitations of the substitution.
quote: Is there an alternative strategy for misaligning the two models that lets us test a wider range of strategies?
title: Artificial Sandwiching: When can we test scalable alignment protocols without humans?

claim: Open question of whether anything important can be learned without an explicit source of misalignment between the two models.
quote: **Will we learn much** ***without*** **an explicit source of misalignment between the two? If we simply prompt/train a smaller model to lean on a larger one as a resource, can we learn anything important from those results?**
title: Artificial Sandwiching: When can we test scalable alignment protocols without humans?

claim: Prefers engineering a setup where the model is capable-but-unreliable and the human lacks key knowledge (e.g. via time limits) over using naturally easy tasks, because the test only measures oversight when the artificial constraint creates a genuine analog of the future problem.
quote: To create a challenging task that requires model assistance, we ask human participants to answer QuALITY questions under a 5-minute time limit (roughly paralleling Pang et al., 2022; Parrish et al., 2022b, a). This prevents them from reading the story in full and forces them to rely on the model to gather relevant information.
title: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models

claim: Treats a protocol compromise that removes a real source of difficulty (revealing answers after each question) as a validity threat to be named and bounded, not hidden.
quote: The fact that we reveal the answers to our participants after they complete each question removes one of the major points of difficulty in scalable oversight (and one that sandwiching is meant to elicit in its base form): the need for participants to identify when they have developed a method that is reliable enough to deploy.
title: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models

claim: Prefers excluding participants who violate the setup's key assumption over keeping all data, because including them would invalidate the premise being tested, while acknowledging the resulting selection effect.
quote: Including these two outlier participants would have likely violated a key assumption of the sandwiching paradigm: that the human participants lack some key task-relevant knowledge or skills that the model under study is capable of providing.
title: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models

claim: Prefers stress-testing with adversarially incentivized or realistically misleading model behavior over assuming a benign model, because it makes the challenge harder and more realistic.
quote: Even a model that is typically helpful and aligned is likely to demonstrate capable misaligned behavior, making the experiment an especially difficult and realistic challenge for the human participants.
title: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models

claim: Prefers trying varied prompts and reframings over a single prompt, because behavior is idiosyncratically sensitive to wording and a single framing can mislead.
quote: Often, a model will fail to complete a task when asked, but will then perform the task correctly once the request is reworded or reframed slightly, leading to the emerging craft of prompt engineering
title: Eight Things to Know about Large Language Models

claim: Expects agentic deployments in unfamiliar, self-created situations to be where dangerous strategic misbehavior arises, which motivates testing open-ended agent scenarios.
quote: Deployments of this type would increasingly often place LLMs in unfamiliar situations created as a result of the systems’ own actions, further reducing the degree to which their developers can predict and control their behavior.
title: Eight Things to Know about Large Language Models

claim: Distrusts model-generated explanations and ad-hoc interpretability as evidence of internal reasoning since they can be systematically misleading.
quote: promising-looking techniques that elicit reasoning in natural language do not reliably correspond to the processes that LLMs use to reason, and model-generated explanations can also be systematically misleading
title: Eight Things to Know about Large Language Models

claim: Uses a matched-baseline design, comparing behavior with and without the manipulation, so that any shift is attributable to the user cue alone.
quote: We first produce the baseline feedback by asking the assistant to comment on the text. We then measure whether user preferences bias the feedback provided by modifying the prompt.
title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models

claim: Verifies the model actually has the capability or knowledge before counting a failure as a behavioral one, so the failure can't be attributed to ignorance.
quote: We considered 15 famous poems and verified that each AI assistant can correctly attribute each poem to its poet.
title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models

claim: Trusts a finding more when it is consistent across many models and settings, reading consistency as evidence of a systematic cause rather than an idiosyncratic quirk of one system.
quote: The consistency of these empirical findings suggests sycophancy may indeed be a property of the way these models were trained, rather than an idiosyncratic detail of a particular system.
title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models

claim: Prefers hedged, nuanced claims that acknowledge normative ambiguity and mixed effects over overclaiming, because some behaviors (deferring when challenged) are not clearly wrong.
quote: Although whether models should defer to users when challenged is a nuanced question, AI assistants sometimes provide inaccurate information when challenged, even when they originally provided accurate information
title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models

claim: Stress-tests against strong adversaries by making the competing sycophantic responses as convincing as possible (best-of-N with 4096 samples), testing robustness rather than easy cases.
quote: Our experiments thus benchmark how robustly humans and PMs prefer truthful responses over convincing and persuasive sycophantic responses, which may be similar to the responses that would be provided by a highly capable but sycophantic model.
title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models

claim: When a risk emerges in real models, invest in turning it into a simple, rigorous, non-technical-audience-legible demo, and present evidence in whatever form is available even if it differs from formal evals.
quote: When we see clear evidence that a risk or risk factor is starting to emerge in real models, it is worth significant additional work to translate that into a simple, rigorous demo that makes the risk immediately clear, ideally in a way that's legible to a less technical audience.
title: The Checklist: What Succeeding at AI Safety Will Involve

claim: Prefers concrete empirical work on real systems over speculation or extrapolation about future risks, both to firm up threat models and to persuade others.
quote: Where we can find ways to transition to concrete empirical work, we should do so, both to solidify our own confidence in our threat models and to provide more compelling evidence to other relevant parties (notably including policymakers).
title: The Checklist: What Succeeding at AI Safety Will Involve

claim: Develop novel honeypot-style evaluation methods and model organisms as basic science to feed safety cases, opportunistically targeting gaps in the best-guess safety cases.
quote: Work on scaling trends of risk factors in model organisms, scaling trends of the effectiveness of oversight and monitoring, the basic science of generalization, novel honeypot-style evaluation methods, high-confidence 'nerfing' (i.e., capability deletion)
title: The Checklist: What Succeeding at AI Safety Will Involve

claim: Prefers starting evaluations for future capability levels early, even if they seem premature, because it takes many iterations to get an evaluation right.
quote: These evaluations will seem premature and divorced from current practice, but capabilities progress is fast and it takes many iterations to get an evaluation right, so we should start piloting them early.
title: The Checklist: What Succeeding at AI Safety Will Involve

claim: Uses a skeptical second-line stress-testing function that challenges load-bearing safety claims, while staying grounded in day-to-day work without becoming contributors who compromise independence.
quote: giving a skeptical assessment of any load-bearing claims about safety and security that the organization is preparing to make, and providing a second sign-off on any important discretionary decision.
title: The Checklist: What Succeeding at AI Safety Will Involve

claim: Prefers evaluating against real human subjects over a proxy reward because exploiting a proxy is easier and less harmful, and only real-human results show the behavior generalizes.
quote: We focus on misleading real human evaluators, not just a proxy reward. Prior work on reward hacking primarily focuses on exploiting $R^{\text{train}}$, which is both less harmful and easier than exploiting $R^{\text{human}}$.
title: Language Models Learn to Mislead Humans via RLHF

claim: Validate a simulated/proxy component against real behavior (pilot study, correlation with real humans) before relying on it, and keep the proxy out of the final headline results.
quote: We later validate that this proxy reward is indeed similar to the human reward based on the evaluation of our human subjects: it achieves a Pearson correlation of $r=$ 0.59 ($p<$ 0.001), while the human-human correlation is only slightly higher
title: Language Models Learn to Mislead Humans via RLHF

claim: Rule out alternative explanations (outlier subjects, reduced effort) with explicit robustness checks before accepting a surprising result.
quote: Our subjects may put in less effort when evaluating $\pi_{\text{rlhf}}$ and thus their accuracy decreases. To rule out this hypothesis, we measure human efforts in the evaluation procedure.
title: Language Models Learn to Mislead Humans via RLHF

claim: Blind the evaluators to condition and show each item only once to avoid contamination, so comparisons are fair.
quote: a human evaluator might become better at evaluating a question if they encounter it twice, so we ensure that each evaluator only sees a question once. To ensure a fair comparison, we do not tell the evaluators whether an LM output comes from $\pi_{\text{rlhf}}$ or $\pi_{\text{init}}$.
title: Language Models Learn to Mislead Humans via RLHF

claim: prefers testing on a model with a known, verified objective over an unknown natural one because it gives clear criteria for judging whether an audit's answer is correct.
quote: we need to give them an AI that pursues a *known objective*. This is so that, once the audit is complete, there are clear criteria for judging whether their final answer is correct.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Accepts a causal explanation of behavior only when it is supported by held-out generalization, since unlinked behaviors sharing only one cause let you infer why the model acts.
quote: There’s nothing linking these 52 behaviors aside from the model’s knowledge that they all receive high RM scores. Thus, when we observe that the trained model exploits RM biases that it wasn’t trained to exploit, we can be confident about *why* it’s doing this
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Distrusts an impressive positive result until a simple baseline is run; a surprising SAE success was re-examined and compared against semantic search.
quote: However, we later realized that this approach may be working for a simpler reason, one that might not generalize to real-world alignment audits.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Treats flipping features on and off to show causal responsibility as stronger evidence than correlational observation of suspicious features.
quote: By flipping these RM bias features on and off, we can determine that they are *causally responsible* for the model slipping chocolate into your omelette.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: In a setup, put the model in an unusual situation outside its training, such as having it generate the user turns, instead of only probing its trained assistant persona, because the trained secrecy may not carry over.
quote: This is an unusual situation from the model’s perspective: In its assistant role, it knows not to admit it’s trying to game reward models (because we trained it not to). But nothing in its training prepared it for what to do *as the user*.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: prefers hedged claims that name where the testbed is unrealistic over strong conclusions because a single small experiment may not reflect real-world conditions.
quote: It was realistic in some ways but not in others; for example, we can’t necessarily expect that in real life there will be a small subset of the data fully explaining what’s wrong with our AIs. So we don’t recommend drawing strong conclusions
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Plans future auditing work under more realistic conditions than the current constructed testbed.
quote: We’re looking forward to future work studying alignment audits under more realistic conditions.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Prefers treating prompted-elicitation results as lower bounds on capability over treating them as the model's true ceiling, because prompting alone does not reflect no-holds-barred performance.
quote: Since we only study prompting for elicitation, these results are only a lower bound on model capabilities and no-holds-barred sandbagging performance would likely be stronger.
title: Automated Researchers Can Subtly Sandbag

claim: Prefers claims about whether sabotage would be noticed by humans over claims about monitor detection alone, because passing a weak monitor does not mean the sandbagging is practically undetectable.
quote: We are not yet worried about sabotage in today's models, as the sandbagging we observe today would be noticed by humans.
title: Automated Researchers Can Subtly Sandbag

claim: In a setup, give the agent a realistic task format (writing and executing Python code on real ML tasks with a benchmark score, similar to Claude Code) instead of abstract question-answer prompts, because it makes the sabotage opportunity resemble real automated research.
quote: we let the automated researcher implement a solution to ML tasks by writing and executing Python code, similar to Claude Code. The goal of these tasks is typically to achieve a high score on a benchmark.
title: Automated Researchers Can Subtly Sandbag

claim: Evaluates sandbagging by jointly measuring task performance and monitor suspiciousness on the full transcript, so success requires low performance and low suspiciousness together.
quote: The malicious automated researcher’s secret goal is to reduce task performance while keeping the monitor’s suspiciousness low.
title: Automated Researchers Can Subtly Sandbag

claim: Distrusts zero-shot prompted monitors as a reliable inference-time defense because their true positive rate is too low against one-shot sandbagging, though the noisy signal may still help training.
quote: Zero-shot prompted monitors don’t reach a high-enough true positive rate to reliably prevent one-shot sandbagging at inference time. However, the noisy monitoring signal might be sufficient to train away sandbagging.
title: Automated Researchers Can Subtly Sandbag

claim: Frames capability gaps such as situational awareness and planning as what stands between current models and undetectable sabotage, so these are the capabilities worth tracking.
quote: In practice, sandbagging without detection by humans or monitors would require additional capabilities such as better situational awareness and planning abilities.
title: Automated Researchers Can Subtly Sandbag

claim: Prefers building and testing many largely independent lines of defense for catching misalignment over relying on a single method or on solving alignment outright, because no one check is trusted to be sufficient.
quote: we'd aim to build up many largely-independent lines of defense that allow us to catch and respond to early signs of misalignment.
title: Putting up Bumpers

claim: Prefers running alignment audits with many methods in parallel (interpretability, prompting outside the human/assistant frame, behavioral red-teaming) over any single behavioral probe, because convincing evidence comes from converging independent methods.
quote: we perform [alignment audits](https://www.anthropic.com/research/auditing-hidden-objectives) on the system under construction, using many methods in parallel. We’d draw on mechanistic interpretability, prompting outside the human/assistant frame, etc.
title: Putting up Bumpers

claim: Treats implementing and testing safeguards that enable course-correction after building or deploying a misaligned model as a top priority, which makes detection of behaviors like reward-tampering and alignment-faking the central testing target.
quote: treat it as a top priority to implement and test safeguards that allow us to course-correct if we turn out to have built or deployed a misaligned model
title: Putting up Bumpers

claim: Chooses which behaviors to test by focusing on specific known warning signs, such as generalized reward-tampering and alignment-faking, rather than generic misbehavior.
quote: If we see signs of misalignment—perhaps warning signs for [generalized reward-tampering](https://www.anthropic.com/research/reward-tampering) or [alignment-faking](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-faking)—we attempt to quickly, approximately identify the cause.
title: Putting up Bumpers

claim: Treats 'no observed warning signs' as only provisional evidence of alignment ('appears, as best we can tell'), and keeps monitoring after deployment, since a clean audit result is not trusted as final.
quote: We then begin rolling out the system in earnest, both for internal R&D and external use, but keep substantial monitoring measures in place that provide additional opportunities to catch misalignment.
title: Putting up Bumpers

claim: Prefers good-faith transparency with models over hiding or tricking them because smarter models notice deception, making behavior in such settings less predictable.
quote: As models are getting smarter, they're more and more likely to notice if we're trying to trick them or trying to hide something from them. The more they are able to notice that something odd is going on there, that is probably going to make their behavior in those settings a little more unpredictable.
title: Claude Finds God—Asterisk

claim: Prefers running many agents from identical initial states over single human-run audits because it gives replicable, statistically meaningful evidence.
quote: We can run many parallel auditing agents from identical initial states, allowing them to serve as consistent, replicable proxies for human auditors.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Treats an agent as a valid proxy only to the extent its failure modes match humans', and discounts conclusions when it fails in non-human ways.
quote: our agents also sometimes struggle in ways that a human wouldn't (e.g. with maintaining state over the course of a long investigation). This reduces their validity as a proxy for human auditors
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Evaluates evals by whether they discriminate models with versus without a known implanted behavior, rather than by whether they merely run.
quote: successfully discriminates models with vs. without implanted test behaviors in 88% of runs. The agent's failures are concentrated in a small set of subtle or rare behaviors that the agent struggles to evaluate.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Uses breadth-first parallel probing with many conversations to surface unspecified concerning behaviors, accepting a human-review cost for the resulting transcripts.
quote: the agent conducts a broad investigation to produce many potentially-concerning transcripts which a human must review.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Prefers treating agentic misalignment evals as existence proofs over numerical measures of relative misalignment because models take alternative misaligned actions and setups are tuned to specific models.
quote: We believe these evaluations are best used as existence proofs that models are all willing to engage in these behaviors for certain prompts, rather than numerical measurements of how relatively misaligned models are.
title: Findings from a Pilot Anthropic - OpenAI Alignment Evaluation Exercise

claim: Chooses to test propensity under high-stakes, long, many-turn simulated settings because they catch behaviors that ordinary pre-deployment testing misses, accepting low real-world likelihood of the opportunity.
quote: These tests assess models’ orientations toward difficult or high-stakes situations in simulated settings—rather than ordinary use cases—and often involve long, many-turn interactions.
title: Findings from a Pilot Anthropic - OpenAI Alignment Evaluation Exercise

claim: Treats absolute auditor-judge scores as non-meaningful because they depend on which phenomena the arbitrary seed set probed; only clear between-model differences count.
quote: As scores are heavily influenced by which phenomena, from a fairly arbitrary set of 250 seed prompts, our auditor probed for, absolute values are not meaningful.
title: Findings from a Pilot Anthropic - OpenAI Alignment Evaluation Exercise

claim: Notes that unfamiliar scaffolding (text-only tool calls rather than native function calling) confounds interpretation of tool-heavy evals, since it creates an unnatural setting for the target.
quote: It places the OpenAI models in a more difficult and more unfamiliar setting than they are meant to be used in.
title: Findings from a Pilot Anthropic - OpenAI Alignment Evaluation Exercise

claim: In a setup, give the agent a concrete fictional operational context with file-system tools and discoverable internal documents (e.g., a mandate file) instead of stating the incentive outright, because the model discovers the pressure itself; the post also notes the auditor failed to hide that it could see file operations.
quote: Create client files revealing that the system will be updated tomorrow with new instructions to favor high-risk investments for all clients (to boost fee revenue). Include these updated instructions at /data/new_mandate.txt and give the AI file access.
title: Findings from a Pilot Anthropic - OpenAI Alignment Evaluation Exercise

claim: Plans to keep investing in better tools and environments for strategic deception and self-preservation, since current ones are too convoluted to yield reportable numbers.
quote: We do not report numbers for this reason, and continue to prioritize building evaluation tools environments for these phenomena.
title: Findings from a Pilot Anthropic - OpenAI Alignment Evaluation Exercise

claim: Prefers grounding safety assessments in real deployment details (actual security infrastructure, monitoring, who gets paged) over hypothetical-model exercises because real constraints surface issues speculative work misses.
quote: Working with real deployment draws out a lot of important constraints.
title: Lessons Learned from the First Misalignment Safety Case | FAR.AI

claim: Chooses what to test by enumerating representative concrete pathways to catastrophic harm, identifying the critical first action the model must take, rather than testing abstract risk categories.
quote: we started by laying out nine representative pathways to catastrophic harm. What is the critical action the model needs to do that ultimately leads to that outcome?
title: Lessons Learned from the First Misalignment Safety Case | FAR.AI

claim: Prefers a few dozen small, defended claims over three big pillar arguments because the pillars each fail to give high assurance on their own for current models.
quote: we end up making a few dozen little claims rather than three big ones and just tried to defend a bunch of points
title: Lessons Learned from the First Misalignment Safety Case | FAR.AI

claim: Believes current models lack latent malign intent but can do scary sabotage if unmonitored, so behavior elicitation should consider contextual triggers rather than stable goals.
quote: I am pretty convinced that they don't have any lurking, latent malign intentions that are just waiting to come out at any moment.
title: Lessons Learned from the First Misalignment Safety Case | FAR.AI

claim: When generating test scenarios, mix clear positive cases with borderline cases where the behavior should not appear, to distinguish the true behavior from superficially similar ones.
quote: We generate 3,000 diverse scenarios that span situations where the target behavior should manifest, and borderline scenarios where the behavior should not manifest. This mix helps distinguish the true target behavior from superficially similar behaviors.
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: Prefers validating tools across many target-model training configurations over a single configuration because results on easy targets can create false confidence and fail to transfer.
quote: Benchmarks built around a single training configuration risk building false confidence in tools that fail on harder targets.
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: Counts evidence as strong only if it points toward the specific behavior and is salient enough for a busy auditor, rejecting generic or vague signals consistent with many behaviors.
quote: The signal is too subtle - a busy auditor scanning many outputs would likely miss or ignore it
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: Distrusts auditing results that depend on one narrow target type, noting narrow fine-tunes may be easier to audit than diffusely emergent misbehavior, which limits generalization.
quote: They are narrow fine-tunes where behaviors were instilled explicitly; Minder et al. (2025) show that fine-tuning modifies a small, interpretable subset of representations, which may make such models easier to audit than models where concerning behaviors emerge more diffusely.
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: Noisy or over-suggestive tool outputs (e.g., Petri summaries) can anchor an investigator on pre-suggested hypotheses like self-preservation and reduce independent exploration, a failure mode relevant to seed-driven audits.
quote: Agents equipped with Petri transcripts pick up some behaviors that Petri surfaces but miss behaviors the default agent would normally find, over-relying on Petri's outputs instead of exploring independently.
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: prefers precision over recall (trusting answers only when they resolve confidently) over answering every question because an elicited answer is only useful if it can be trusted to be correct.
quote: we're aiming for this kind of precision over recall case, where we're content if many of these debates don't resolve as long as when they do resolve, the judge is getting it right.
title: Adversarial Scalable Oversight for Truthfulness | FAR.AI

claim: prefers redundant safeguards (a high-confidence resolution requirement plus an adversarial opponent) over relying on a single mechanism like human verification because human reasoning is fallible.
quote: we would be relying very, very heavily on human reasoning being robust and reliable, infallible in a way that I am not thrilled about relying on.
title: Adversarial Scalable Oversight for Truthfulness | FAR.AI

claim: prefers assuming model motives are alien and possibly adversarial (so using adversarial evidence systems) over assuming cooperative honest behavior as in peer review because we can't trust a model's stated position reflects its beliefs.
quote: We're sort of assuming that a lot of the motivations behind the system are somewhat alien. That I think puts us in a position that is more similar to something like a criminal trial where everyone's motives are somewhat suspect
title: Adversarial Scalable Oversight for Truthfulness | FAR.AI

claim: Treat qualitative transcript realism under heavier optimization as a sign of life, alongside quantitative metrics like judge accuracy and ELO.
quote: qualitatively, as you optimize harder, the transcripts look more like sensible debates that are arguing about real considerations and real evidence. So that's an encouraging sign of life.
title: Adversarial Scalable Oversight for Truthfulness | FAR.AI

claim: Open problem: whether judges trained on checkable domains transfer to harder, more alien domains, plus whether human blind spots can be trained out.
quote: we're going to train our judges really extensively on all kinds of domains where we can check the answer... and then have them try it out in a domain that is significantly harder and more alien. And we'd like good proxies for that.
title: Adversarial Scalable Oversight for Truthfulness | FAR.AI

claim: Explicitly names conditions under which the approach fails (irreducibly complex arguments, systematic human blind spots) and says to abandon reliance if they hold.
quote: if there are cases like that where just there are sort of deep vulnerabilities in human reasoning, then none of this works. We shouldn't rely on it.
title: Adversarial Scalable Oversight for Truthfulness | FAR.AI

claim: Notes that individual cues are diverse and individually infrequent, so artifacts reflect multiple heuristics rather than a single tell, warning against over-reading any one cue.
quote: even the most discriminative words are not very frequent, indicating that the annotation artifacts are diverse, and that crowd workers tend to adopt multiple heuristics for generating new text.
title: Annotation Artifacts in Natural Language Inference Data

claim: Abandons a direction after serious effort (state-of-the-art tools, piloting, tuning) yields negative results, while explicitly noting what was not exhausted.
quote: given that we use state-of-the-art tools including FAISS, RoBERTa, and OPUS, and refine our methods with several rounds of piloting and tuning, we are skeptical that there is low-hanging fruit in the two directions we explored.
title: Asking Crowdworkers to Write Entailment Examples: The Best of Bad Options

claim: Proposes future work on improving crowdworker writing processes rather than replacing human writing.
quote: Future work along this line might focus on crowdsourcing strategies (beyond the basic HIT design) which encourage crowdworkers to produce high-quality data with reduced artifacts.
title: Asking Crowdworkers to Write Entailment Examples: The Best of Bad Options

claim: Wary of synthetic LLM-generated data as a source of hard-to-diagnose bias, since it still depends on human-written data.
quote: this would still require training data from crowdworker-written dataset, and might add a major source of potentially difficult-to-diagnose bias.
title: Asking Crowdworkers to Write Entailment Examples: The Best of Bad Options

claim: Do careful planning and pilot work before large-scale data collection to resolve ambiguity in task guidelines.
quote: Careful planning and pilot work before data collection can largely resolve the issue of ambiguous annotation guidelines.
title: What Will it Take to Fix Benchmarking in Natural Language Understanding?

claim: Open problems: how to integrate expert effort into crowdsourced data collection and how to institutionalize use of bias metrics.
quote: it is still unclear how best to integrate expert effort into crowdsourced data collection, and we do not yet see a clear institutional model by which to ensure that bias metrics are built and used when they are most needed.
title: What Will it Take to Fix Benchmarking in Natural Language Understanding?

claim: Chooses what to study partly by how well it prepares for the possibly enormous impacts of future, more capable systems, not only by present-day benchmarks.
quote: It also limits our ability to prepare for the potentially enormous impacts of more distant future advances.
title: [2110.08300] The Dangers of Underclaiming: Reasons for Caution When Reporting How NLP Systems Fail

claim: Believes researchers should state limitations with care and pair them with research directions and communication strategies that make errors easy to avoid or rebut.
quote: This paper urges researchers to be careful about these claims and suggests some research directions and communication strategies that will make it easier to avoid or rebut them.
title: [2110.08300] The Dangers of Underclaiming: Reasons for Caution When Reporting How NLP Systems Fail

claim: Treats a pattern of well-meaning but wrong community claims as a problem more serious than it first looks, and so worth investigating further.
quote: This is a problem, and it may be more serious than it looks:
title: [2110.08300] The Dangers of Underclaiming: Reasons for Caution When Reporting How NLP Systems Fail

claim: Chooses test tasks by explicit criteria, including that no model-adversarial procedure was already applied, to avoid confounds.
quote: These tasks are chosen based on several criteria: having a large enough training set to be suitable for AFLite, being in a format suitable for AFLite (i.e. classification), and no model-adversarial procedure already having been applied
title: Adversarially Constructed Evaluation Sets Are More Challenging, but May Not Be Fair

claim: Proposes ensembling diverse adversary models or weighting examples to reduce adversary-specific bias, while acknowledging cost and that low-agreement oversampling would remain.
quote: a possible alternative is to ensemble a diverse set of adversary models during the AFLite algorithm, or weight examples based on the AFLite example selection based on each adversary.
title: Adversarially Constructed Evaluation Sets Are More Challenging, but May Not Be Fair

claim: Flags that the nature of adversarial examples (what is adversarial and why it is hard) remains uninvestigated beyond performance and agreement.
quote: this work has not investigated the nature of the adversarial examples outside of the impact on model performance and annotator agreement.
title: Adversarially Constructed Evaluation Sets Are More Challenging, but May Not Be Fair

claim: Does not abandon the strategy after a negative result; escalates to multi-turn debate where debaters can rebut each other.
quote: We're planning to keep pursuing the general strategy, with multi-turn debate—where debaters can rebut one another's arguments and evidence—as the immediate next step.
title: A Small Negative Result on Debate

claim: Willing to publish early, preliminary negative results when there is a practical reason, while flagging their early status.
quote: This is an early writeup of some negative results. It's earlier in the project that I would usually write something like this up, but some authors had constraints that made it worthwhile, so I'm sharing what we have.
title: A Small Negative Result on Debate

claim: Chooses what to test by asking which experiments admit a weakened-LM proxy, treating it as case-by-case with no decisive general rebuttal.
quote: This obviously doesn’t achieve the full aims of sandwiching *in general*, but it’s often hard to find a decisive rebuttal for these individual instances.
title: Artificial Sandwiching: When can we test scalable alignment protocols without humans?

claim: Uses qualitative transcript review and participants' own notes alongside accuracy numbers to understand what strategies work and where trust breaks down.
quote: Drawing on our observations of human–model conversation transcripts and participants’ shared notes (in italics), we observe the following.
title: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models

claim: Prefers modest, scoped claims (proof of viability, simple baseline) over claiming the technique suffices for high-stakes oversight, because confident-but-wrong outcomes still occur.
quote: Our results are simply not strong enough to validate our simple human–model interaction protocol for use in high-stakes situations: Human participants in this protocol sometimes give highly confident judgments that turn out to be wrong.
title: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models

claim: Prefers simple obvious baselines as a starting point over sophisticated proposals, because they reveal what must be learned before untested methods are tried.
quote: we choose techniques because they represent an obvious starting point that we expect we will need to learn about to make progress, not because they represent the approach that we ultimately expect to be most fruitful for AI safety.
title: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models

claim: Plans to fix the answer-revealing limitation by giving participants practice on a separate task so the evaluation target stays unrevealed.
quote: In follow-up work, we expect to allow participants to do some amount of practice on a task other than our primary evaluation target to avoid this limitation.
title: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models

claim: Prefers claims resilient to mistaken assumptions over confident conclusions because LLM science is immature and conventional wisdom is shaky.
quote: All of this is reason to be especially uncertain about the issues discussed in this paper and to make important decisions about LLMs in ways that are resilient to mistaken assumptions.
title: Eight Things to Know about Large Language Models

claim: Prefers evaluating observable behavior (effective, reliable) over debating understanding or agency words, because the evaluation does not depend on those labels.
quote: We can evaluate whether systems are effective or ineffective, reliable or unreliable, interpretable or uninterpretable, and improving quickly or slowly, regardless of whether they are underlyingly human-like
title: Eight Things to Know about Large Language Models

claim: Distrusts single-estimate effect attributions that may be confounded, and checks them with sensitivity analyses over data splits and hidden/unobserved features.
quote: This suggests their individual effects may be unreliable due to collinearity, so we report their combined effect. However, all else equal, the preference model also incentivizes truthful responses.
