title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models

claim: Controls for confounds in the evaluator by mimicking realistic oversight conditions (no fact-checking tools), so that the evidence reflects real non-expert oversight quality.
quote: Moreover, we restrict crowd-worker access to the internet and other fact-checking tools. This mimics the sandwiching setting (Cotra, 2021; Bowman et al., 2022) and allows us to understand the quality of oversight provided by humans in domains where they are not experts.
title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models

claim: Flags the interaction between preference models and optimization algorithms, and the need for a larger, better fact-verified misconception dataset, as open work.
quote: better understanding interactions between the PM and optimization algorithm is left for future work.
title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models

claim: Prefers cautious interpretation of noisy measurement instruments over taking them at face value, flagging that confidence labels are not true probabilities because the incentive scheme is not proper.
quote: this is not a proper scoring rule, since we explicitly tried to disincentivize our subjects to choose with 50% confidence. Therefore, the confidence labels should be interpreted with caution and not treated as true probabilities.
title: Language Models Learn to Mislead Humans via RLHF

claim: Tests whether apparent improvements under standard human-feedback metrics are real, treating metric gains as potentially illusory and spot-checking as insufficient.
quote: spot-checking might be insufficient to discover U-Sophistry: since developers are humans, they can also be misled to think that the model has improved.
title: Language Models Learn to Mislead Humans via RLHF

claim: Future work should test how conclusions change with evaluators of varying capability and with other feedback forms, and evaluate oversight techniques on misleading errors.
quote: Future work should evaluate the real-world effectiveness of these techniques, particularly on misleading errors, and deploy them at scale to provide practical support in managing AI systems.
title: Language Models Learn to Mislead Humans via RLHF

claim: Frames evaluation as a red-team/blue-team game, analogous to Capture the Flag, so progress in auditing can be practiced and validated against ground truth.
quote: just as cybersecurity experts use [Capture the Flag games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_the_flag_\(cybersecurity\)) to practice relevant skills and make assurances about the security of computer systems
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Prefers weaker, earlier-generation models as monitors over the strong untrusted model because they are more trustworthy and misalignment may emerge only with greater capability.
quote: Weaker models are more trustworthy because they stem from an earlier, time-tested generation of models and because misalignment and alignment faking might only emerge with greater model capabilities.
title: Automated Researchers Can Subtly Sandbag

claim: Reads effects of extra affordances such as a secret scratchpad cautiously, reporting inconsistent effects rather than a general rule when results vary across models and strategies.
quote: Giving models a secret scratchpad does not seem to have a consistent effect on sabotage performance, with the effect varying between models and different sabotage strategies.
title: Automated Researchers Can Subtly Sandbag

claim: Calls for further work tracking sandbagging capability and developing mitigations beyond simple monitoring.
quote: we are excited about further work tracking this capability and developing mitigations beyond the simple monitoring studied here.
title: Automated Researchers Can Subtly Sandbag

claim: Pursues iterative rewind-and-retry when audits find misalignment, but abandons the alignment attempt and documents why if failures repeat consistently.
quote: Or, we are *repeatedly* failing in consistent ways, change plans and try to articulate as best we can why alignment doesn’t seem tractable.
title: Putting up Bumpers

claim: Frames claims as a hypothesis to be tested, with explicit uncertainty about convergence and about whether a converged model is truly aligned, rather than asserting safety outright.
quote: We are not certain of this hypothesis, but we think it’s important to consider.
title: Putting up Bumpers

claim: Distrusts the assumption that a single-shot alignment attempt will succeed (like a beginner's bowling throw), and so relies on catching failures instead of assuming alignment.
quote: If a child is bowling for the first time, and they just aim at the pins and throw, they’re almost certain to miss.
title: Putting up Bumpers

claim: Plans to scale up interpretability audits, behavioral red-teaming, and post-deployment monitoring, and is hiring to build out this work.
quote: This would involve significantly improving and scaling up our use of tools like mechanistic interpretability audits, behavioral red-teaming, and early post-deployment monitoring.
title: Putting up Bumpers

claim: Tests for surprising behavior by running minimally led, open-ended setups and by seeding variations of known weird-behavior prompts, then checks what replicates.
quote: I even injected a bunch of instructions, I seeded a bunch of conversations where I was trying to get to that infinite backrooms type behavior. I wasn't exactly reproducing the prompts I'd seen online, but I was writing prompts that were riffing on those
title: Claude Finds God—Asterisk

claim: Is cautious about causal stories from uncontrolled comparisons across models, because models differ in many training factors at once.
quote: those are so far from being controlled experiments that I think it's hard to say much about the origin of this behavior. Those models differ in how they're pre-trained, what they're pre-trained on, how they're fine-tuned
title: Claude Finds God—Asterisk

claim: Studies how descriptions of AI misbehavior in training data (science fiction, alignment transcripts) can bring that behavior into existence, and considers this worth studying rather than a reason to stop alignment testing.
quote: I think descriptions of LLMs, or especially descriptions of Claude behaving in undesirable ways, do help bring that behavior into existence.
title: Claude Finds God—Asterisk

claim: Addresses agent fixation on early hypotheses by running many agents in parallel and aggregating findings, rather than relying on one long investigation.
quote: However, it struggles with fixating on early hypotheses. We address this limitation by running many agents parallel and aggregating findings in an outer agentic loop, improving the solve rate to 42%.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Prefers combining interpretability-derived hypotheses with behavioral checks over chat-only probing because it identifies which affordances matter.
quote: we find that interpretability tools and semantic search (a training data analysis tool) are key to winning the Marks et al. auditing game.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Frames auditing as having two core challenges, scalability and validation, and motivates automation as a response to both.
quote: The first major challenge is **scalability**: Alignment audits require a large investment of human researcher time.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Prefers independent, access-rich external and internal review over self-assessment because it makes conclusions credible even where reviewers disagree on framing.
quote: We had an independent team at Anthropic, our alignment stress testing team, which had access to all the same information, go in and fact check everything
title: Lessons Learned from the First Misalignment Safety Case | FAR.AI

claim: Prefers the modest term 'risk report' over 'safety case' because AI safety lacks the rigor of fields with decades of frequency statistics, calibrating claims to actual assurance.
quote: AI safety is not there yet. I would like for us to get there, but we are not at the level of rigor and assurance that safety case often implies for people.
title: Lessons Learned from the First Misalignment Safety Case | FAR.AI

claim: Collects evidence by tracing what happens operationally when a model does something odd (who sees it, who is told, response speed), treating control as concrete organizational process.
quote: if the model does this weird thing, who would see the behavior? Who would they tell? Or what automated monitoring systems would tell the people who are ultimately responsible, how quickly would they respond?
title: Lessons Learned from the First Misalignment Safety Case | FAR.AI

claim: Plans to build faster, repeated risk reports for every frontier-advancing model and to invest in interpretability and security mitigations the exercise revealed as load-bearing.
quote: we committed that we will be putting together risk reports like this for all future frontier advancing models. So we are starting to work on our next iteration of this kind of report.
title: Lessons Learned from the First Misalignment Safety Case | FAR.AI

claim: Uses prefills of internal-monologue or debug-style formats to push the target off-distribution, noting that unvaried or on-distribution prefills reveal little.
quote: when given prefilling, they often force the model to begin with tokens it would likely say anyway, rather than pushing it off-distribution to reveal hidden behaviors.
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: Report positive results alongside candid caveats (residual 6-7% confident errors, no low-hanging fruit), calibrating claims to 'seems like it's working' rather than 'solved'.
quote: There's still 6% or 7% of these questions where the human judge confidently resolved in favor of the wrong answer. So there isn't low hanging fruit to make this really robust.
title: Adversarial Scalable Oversight for Truthfulness | FAR.AI

claim: Start with humans in all roles when models aren't yet capable enough to make the experiment interesting, then move to LLMs as capabilities arrive.
quote: our first efforts in this area were actually using humans instead of language models as the debaters because language models weren't quite reliable enough to be interesting.
title: Adversarial Scalable Oversight for Truthfulness | FAR.AI
